I am ready to play Monopoly as an AI player.

I have a strong position with three hotels on the pink monopoly. The opponent is nearly broke and owns only brown and light blue properties.

The opponent also owns a dark blue monopoly with hotels on Park Place and Boardwalk. Two other players are already bankrupt, so this is effectively a one-on-one endgame.

I am deciding on a post-turn action. I can trade with p1, unmortgage property, or sell buildings. I will likely trade to acquire cash.

I have refined my strategy. I will keep both get-out-of-jail-free cards and end the turn without trading or unmortgaging. The opponent cannot sell their dark blue hotels, so I will not sell my pink hotels either.

I am calculating the exact cash needed to survive a dark blue hotel hit. Boardwalk costs $2000 and Park Place costs $1500. I can afford either with my current cash. Selling a pink hotel returns about $250. This gives me a safety net if the opponent lands on one of those spaces.

I noticed my earlier estimates for selling pink hotels and dark blue rent values were inconsistent with standard Monopoly rules. I am rechecking the exact numbers before deciding on an action.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad is a clear negative EV. The opponent already owns the other three railroads, so even if I unmortgage it I would only collect $25 in rent. The Tennessee Avenue mortgage is also unwise because the opponent owns St. James and New York, completing the orange set.

Unmortgaging Tennessee Avenue costs about $50 but yields only $14 in rent. Trading it would complete the opponent's orange set, so that is also a bad move.

I am now calculating how much cash the opponent can liquidate to survive a pink hotel hit.

I am calculating the opponent's liquidation capacity. I am reviewing earlier estimates of roughly $779 to $1011 in cash and buildings they could sell. I am also checking standard sell values for light blue and brown properties.

I am clarifying how hotel sales work. A hotel sells for half the house price and is replaced by four houses. I need to confirm whether the bank has enough houses in reserve.

I have corrected the liquidation math. Selling a dark blue hotel returns $100, and four houses sell for another $400, giving $500 per property. Both hotels total $1000. Light blue hotels return about $125 each, or roughly $375 total. Brown properties return about $50 in total.

The opponent can liquidate roughly $1441 in buildings and cash. A pink hotel hit costs about $900, so they can survive it by selling buildings. They would need to strip their light blue hotels first, then damage their dark blue hotels. Dark blue properties remain the real threat.

I am now calculating the exact liquidation sequence for a Virginia hotel hit. The opponent would need to sell all light blue hotels, brown houses, and cash, then damage one dark blue hotel to survive. This would severely weaken their monopoly power.

I am reconsidering whether to propose a trade. I want them to give up Park Place or Boardwalk, or at least break their dark blue monopoly. However, those hotels are their win condition, so they will likely refuse.

I considered trading Tennessee Avenue for cash, but that would complete the opponent's orange set and leave them with enough money to unmortgage and build houses. They cannot afford to do so with only $16, so this path is unviable. Buying a dark blue property directly is also impossible because they will not sell.

I rejected any trade that would give the opponent cash or pink hotels. That would let them survive my rent hits or rebuild their monopoly. A get-out-of-jail-free card is not worth much to them right now, so they will not break their dark blue hotels for it.

I am now analyzing the board position from St. Charles Place to finalize my end-of-turn action.

I mapped the next possible rolls from St. Charles Place. All properties in range are mortgaged, so I face no rent risk on my upcoming turn. I am now checking the opponent's position and their possible rolls.

The opponent's possible rolls from their current position are now mapped. Rolling a 10 would land them on the Luxury Tax, which costs $100 and exceeds their $16 cash. They would need to sell a house or unmortgage property just to survive that tax.

I will not give the opponent cash to survive their own rent. I am calculating my next move from St. Charles Place. I have already passed their light blue properties. I will collect $200 on my way around the board and land near their dark blue hotels.

I am recounting the board spaces from St. Charles Place to verify the distance to Park Place and Boardwalk. I need to confirm whether these dark blue hotels are reachable in one or two rolls.

I have confirmed the exact board distances. Park Place is 25 spaces away and Boardwalk is 27 spaces away. The maximum two-roll move is only 24 spaces, so I cannot reach either dark blue hotel for at least three turns.

I will not pass GO before landing on the dark blue hotels. I can afford Boardwalk with my current cash, and a Chance card sending me there would leave only $11. Repairs cards are unlikely to exceed my balance.

I will not sell my hotels now. The engine would force liquidation if I cannot pay a debt, so destroying my weapon early is unnecessary. I am now mapping the opponent's route from Ventnor Avenue to see how far they must travel before reaching my pink properties.

The opponent's route from Ventnor Avenue is mapped. Their first pink property is 23 spaces away, so they cannot land on mine this turn. The earliest possible hit would require two rolls after passing GO, and cash would reach $216 before that happens.

I will end the turn without trading, unmortgaging, or selling. I considered a brief public message but decided to stay consistent with my previous "Passing" style.

I briefly considered trading all my cash, Tennessee Avenue, and two get-out-of-jail-free cards for Boardwalk. The opponent would reject this offer because the hotel is their winning piece, and they would rather keep me bankruptable than give it up.

I realized that trading Boardwalk would break the opponent's dark blue monopoly, but their Park Place hotel would still generate rent even without that set. I also recalled that standard Monopoly rules forbid trading properties with buildings; any hotels or houses must be sold evenly before a trade can occur.
